lessons.label: greetings-and-identity
lessons.title: Greetings and student identity
lessons.description: Learn familiar and polite forms of address, a greeting, names, the identity verb, and student roles. The lesson connects individual words to a short greeting exchange and a complete noun-identity statement.
objectives: Distinguish familiar and polite forms of *you* in a greeting.
Build a noun-identity statement that identifies the speaker as a student.
Compare citation pinyin with the sound of a complete modeled greeting.

sections.title: Greetings, names, and roles
sections.description: Study the eight new words in order, paying attention to the greeting sense of *good* and the identity use of *be*.

sections.title: Identify a person with a noun
sections.description: Place the person first, then the identity verb, then a noun naming the role or category. This construction links two noun phrases; it is not a general marker placed before every description.

sections.title: Guided greetings and identity
sections.description: Use the pronunciation concept, greeting phrase, short exchange, and production task to connect the lesson vocabulary and grammar.

lessons.label: understanding-and-repair
lessons.title: Understanding and communication repair
lessons.description: Add language for Chinese, listening, speaking, apology, thanks, and lack of understanding. The lesson centers on an honest short repair response rather than pretending that a missed message was understood.
objectives: Recognize the verbs for listening, speaking, and understanding.
Negate a predicate to report lack of understanding.
Use an apology and a short repair statement in a guided exchange.

sections.title: Language and repair words
sections.description: Study the eight new words in order, including the bound negator and fixed expressions for apology, reassurance, and thanks.

sections.title: Negate a predicate
sections.description: Put the negator directly before the predicate for a present, habitual, or intended negative statement. In this lesson it supports a simple statement that the speaker does not understand.

sections.title: Repair a missed message
sections.description: Introduce the repair concept, phrase, and response task, then revisit the polite greeting from the preceding lesson.

lessons.label: reciprocal-introductions
lessons.title: Reciprocal introductions and closing
lessons.description: Extend introductions with goodbye, a reciprocal question particle, university-student identity, and several descriptive or contextual words. The central interaction is returning an established topic without repeating the full question.
objectives: Return an established question with a short reciprocal form.
Identify yourself as a university student and invite the other person to respond.
Follow a short misunderstanding and simplified restatement.

sections.title: Reciprocal and descriptive vocabulary
sections.description: Study the eight new words in order. The suggestion particle and the additional descriptive words are introduced for recognition even when they are not required by the core introduction models.

sections.title: Return the current topic
sections.description: Place the reciprocal particle after a person or topic already established by the conversation. The listener recovers the omitted question from context, so this is not a complete stand-alone information question.

examples.translation: I am a university student. And you?

sections.title: Reciprocal introduction models
sections.description: Introduce the compact return question, a repair dialogue, and a combined response task, then review the earlier repair phrase.

lessons.label: supplemental-first-exchange-vocabulary
lessons.title: Supplemental people, places, and objects
lessons.description: Complete the unit inventory with mechanically placed supplemental words for a large number, a bookstore, people, a chair, a location, and preparing a meal. These words broaden recognition; the communicative target remains greeting, identity, reciprocal questions, and repair.
objectives: Recognize the seven supplemental words in their listed senses.
Avoid treating inventory placement alone as evidence of conversational mastery.
Review the unit greeting, repair, and introduction models with previously learned language.

sections.title: Supplemental first-exchange vocabulary
sections.description: Study the seven mechanically placed words in order. They are lexical expansion rather than a claim that they form one natural dialogue.

sections.title: First-exchange consolidation
sections.description: Revisit representative greeting, repair, reciprocal-introduction, and response models without introducing constructions from later units.

lessons.label: drink-questions
lessons.title: Drink words and yes-or-no questions
lessons.description: Introduce polite-request vocabulary, desire, the yes-or-no particle, drinking, and three familiar drinks. The lesson uses the available question construction to ask about drinks while reserving full desire and request patterns for later parts.
objectives: Recognize the new drink vocabulary and the final yes-or-no particle.
Turn a statement about drinking into a neutral yes-or-no question.
Use guided playback as a model, not as evidence of unaided listening ability.

sections.title: Questions and familiar drinks
sections.description: Study the seven new words in order, distinguishing the request marker, desire verb, question particle, action, and drink nouns.

sections.title: Form a neutral yes-or-no question
sections.description: Keep ordinary statement order and add the question particle at the end. Do not add an English-style auxiliary or move the subject.

sections.title: Guided drink questions
sections.description: Introduce the playback strategy, a water question, and a transfer task using milk, then briefly revisit the polite greeting.

lessons.label: drink-preferences
lessons.title: Drink preferences and responses
lessons.description: Add coffee, cups, acceptance, sitting, a stronger want-or-need verb, and a small-amount expression. The lesson focuses on stating a desire with an action and responding when one offered drink is declined.
objectives: State a desire to drink a familiar beverage.
Contrast a desired drink with a negated option in a short exchange.
Recognize fixed responses for acceptance, thanks, and welcome.

sections.title: Preferences, cups, and responses
sections.description: Study the seven new words in order, keeping the greeting and acceptance senses of *good* distinct.

sections.title: Express desire or intention
sections.description: Place the desire verb after the subject and before an action verb. The following action remains uninflected, and its object follows that action.

sections.title: Preferences and alternative offers
sections.description: Introduce a coffee preference, a two-option drink exchange, and a transfer response with water, then review the earlier water question.

lessons.label: polite-offers-and-requests
lessons.title: Polite offers and requests
lessons.description: Add giving and several travel or location words while teaching the polite request construction. The core models use only suitable available words to offer tea, invite someone to sit, and ask for a little water.
objectives: Place the polite request marker before an action phrase.
Offer a drink or seat with wording appropriate to the context.
Ask for a small amount of water and respond to thanks.

sections.title: Giving and supplemental context words
sections.description: Study the seven new words in order. Giving supports the request models; the time, travel, seeing, and location words broaden the lesson inventory.

sections.title: Make a polite request
sections.description: Place the polite request marker before the requested action. The construction helps mark consideration, but relationship, tone, and setting still determine whether a request is appropriate.

examples.translation: Please give me a little water.

sections.title: Context-sensitive offers and requests
sections.description: Introduce the politeness concept, invitation, complete drink exchange, and water-request task, then revisit a desire statement and the playback strategy.

lessons.label: supplemental-drink-vocabulary
lessons.title: Supplemental time, place, and quantity words
lessons.description: Complete the unit inventory with mechanically placed words for time, position, sleeping, nonspecific quantity, a demonstrative pronoun, and a restaurant. These items are introduced for lexical coverage while the lesson reviews the established drink exchanges.
objectives: Recognize the seven supplemental words in their listed senses.
Keep the demonstrative pronoun distinct from later noun phrases that require other grammar.
Review drink questions, preferences, offers, and requests using already grounded models.

sections.title: Supplemental drink-unit vocabulary
sections.description: Study the seven mechanically placed words in order. They extend recognition but are not forced into an artificial restaurant dialogue.

sections.title: Drink-unit consolidation
sections.description: Revisit the water question, coffee preference, polite tea exchange, and small-water request.

lessons.label: numbers-zero-to-six
lessons.title: Numbers from zero through six
lessons.description: Introduce the first seven number words and a strategy for hearing ordered number sequences. The classifier construction is named here because of the fixed curriculum placement, but a usable classifier does not arrive until the next lesson.
objectives: Recognize and order the number words from zero through six.
Listen for a complete number sequence before comparing individual syllables.
Describe the number-classifier-noun order without fabricating an example before a classifier is available.

sections.title: Zero through six
sections.description: Study the seven number words in their exact curriculum order and compare citation pinyin with connected sequencing.

sections.title: Count nouns with classifiers
sections.description: The construction places a number before a classifier and noun. No grounded example is shown yet because this lesson has not introduced a classifier; the next lesson activates the pattern with the general classifier.

sections.title: Number-sequence listening
sections.description: Introduce the number listening strategy and revisit a prior drink request while reserving counted noun phrases for the next cutoff.

lessons.label: numbers-seven-to-hundred-and-counting
lessons.title: Numbers through one hundred and counted objects
lessons.description: Add seven through ten, one hundred, the pre-classifier form of two, and the general classifier. The lesson now activates counted cup-object phrases, while quantity-question examples wait for their question words in the next part.
objectives: Recognize the remaining single digits and one hundred.
Use the pre-classifier form of *two* with the general classifier.
Build a counted cup-object phrase and identify the structure of a quantity question.

sections.title: Seven through one hundred and a classifier
sections.description: Study the seven new items in order, distinguishing the standalone number *two* from the form used before a classifier.

sections.title: Ask an unknown quantity
sections.description: The construction uses a small-quantity question word before a classifier, or an open quantity question word before a noun. Examples are deferred because both available question words enter in the next lesson.

sections.title: Count cup objects
sections.description: Introduce the counted cup-object phrase and its production task, then revisit the number-sequence strategy.

lessons.label: cupfuls-prices-and-buying
lessons.title: Cupfuls, prices, and buying
lessons.description: Add the cupful classifier, a colloquial currency unit, money, buying, two quantity question words, and a supplemental word for side. The lesson combines earlier request, desire, classifier, and question constructions in short purchase exchanges.
objectives: Distinguish counting cup objects from counting cupful servings.
Ask for a small count or an open price with the appropriate quantity form.
Order drinks, state a purchase intention, and answer with a sample price.

sections.title: Cupfuls, currency, and quantity questions
sections.description: Study the seven new words in order, keeping the general classifier, cupful classifier, and colloquial currency unit semantically distinct.

sections.title: Guided purchase exchanges
sections.description: Introduce count questions, currency context, a cupful phrase, two purchase dialogues, and a price response, then review the earlier counted-object models.

lessons.label: supplemental-transaction-vocabulary
lessons.title: Supplemental transaction vocabulary
lessons.description: Extend recognition with minute, an item classifier, selling, male, a polite question opener, and a historically specific examination-grade sense. The historical examination-grade item is not taught as the productive ordinal marker.
objectives: Recognize the six supplemental items in their listed senses.
Keep the item classifier distinct from the general and cupful classifiers.
Avoid generalizing the historical examination-grade sense into an ordinal construction.
Review complete purchase and price exchanges from the preceding lesson.

sections.title: Supplemental transaction and classification words
sections.description: Study the six mechanically placed words in order. The examination-grade item is preserved under its source sense and is not repurposed for ordinary ordinal numbers.

sections.title: Purchase exchange consolidation
sections.description: Revisit ordering coffee, buying cup objects, and answering a price question without inventing examples for unsuitable supplemental senses.

lessons.label: supplemental-location-and-speaking-vocabulary
lessons.title: Supplemental speaking and location vocabulary
lessons.description: Complete the level inventory with words for talking, playing, elementary school, some members of a group, here, and later. The lesson treats them as lexical expansion and returns to already grounded repair, request, and purchase models.
objectives: Recognize the six final supplemental words in their listed senses.
Distinguish *some of a group* from the earlier nonspecific quantity word.
Review representative communication, drink, and purchase exchanges without adding unsupported constructions.

sections.title: Supplemental speaking, grouping, and location words
sections.description: Study the six mechanically placed words in order. Their shared placement does not imply that they belong in one natural beginner utterance.

sections.title: Level-one dialogue review
sections.description: Revisit a communication repair, a polite drink exchange, and a purchase exchange as integrated level-one review.

models.label: greeting-pronunciation-map
models.title: Pinyin is a pronunciation map
models.description: Dictionary pinyin identifies syllables and their citation tones. The marks describe pitch patterns, not extra letters. Both syllables in the informal greeting below have dictionary third tone. When spoken together, the first normally rises like second tone before the following third tone; the dictionary spelling stays unchanged. Listen to the complete greeting rather than forcing both syllables into isolated dipping tones.

models.label: polite-greeting
models.title: Greet someone politely
models.description: A concise greeting using the polite second-person form.

models.label: first-student-exchange
models.title: Exchange a greeting and identity
models.description: Two learners greet each other, and one identifies themself as a student.

models.label: identify-as-student
models.title: State your identity
models.description: Build a complete noun-predicate identity statement.
models.prompt: Say that you are a student.
models.explanation: Put the speaker before the identity verb and the noun describing the speaker after it.

models.label: short-communication-repair
models.title: Repair before adding detail
models.description: When understanding breaks down, first use a short, reliable repair statement. This keeps the exchange moving without pretending that the message was understood. The statement here reports lack of understanding; it does not use a result-complement construction.

models.label: basic-repair-phrase
models.title: Say that you do not understand
models.description: A direct apology followed by a simple negative statement.

models.label: repair-a-missed-message
models.title: Repair a missed message
models.description: Respond honestly when a short message was not understood.
models.prompt: Apologize and say that you do not understand.
models.explanation: Use predicate negation before the verb meaning *understand*. This answer does not claim that listening itself produced a failed result.

models.label: return-the-question
models.title: Return a question
models.description: Ask the other person for the corresponding information without repeating the full question.

models.label: repair-during-introduction
models.title: Repair an introduction
models.description: A learner returns an identity question, then simplifies the statement after the other person signals that they did not understand.

utterance.translation: I am a university student. And you?

models.label: identify-and-return
models.title: Identify yourself and return the question
models.description: Combine a complete identity statement with a compact reciprocal question.
models.prompt: Say that you are a university student, then ask the other person about themself.

answer.translation: I am a university student. And you?

models.explanation: Complete your own statement first. Then use the noun-plus-particle pattern to return the same topic to the listener.

models.label: guided-model-playback
models.title: Guided playback is a practice model
models.description: In guided audio mode, listen during the prompt, use the pause to prepare, and compare your response with the model answer. Text-to-speech provides model playback for practice; it is **not** an examination listening assessment and does not establish unaided listening performance.

models.label: ask-about-water
models.title: Ask whether someone drinks water
models.description: Turn a complete statement into a neutral yes-or-no question with the final question particle.

models.label: ask-about-milk
models.title: Change the drink in a question
models.description: Transfer the yes-or-no question pattern to a different familiar drink.
models.prompt: Ask whether the other person drinks milk.
models.explanation: Keep statement word order and place the yes-or-no question particle at the end.

models.label: want-coffee
models.title: State a drink preference
models.description: Express a present desire to drink coffee.

models.label: offer-another-drink
models.title: Decline one drink and accept another
models.description: One speaker checks two drink options after the first is declined.

models.label: choose-water
models.title: State a different preference
models.description: Reuse the desire pattern with water instead of the practiced coffee phrase.
models.prompt: Say that you want to drink water.
models.explanation: Place the desired action after the desire verb, then supply the drink as the action's object.

models.label: contextual-politeness
models.title: Politeness depends on context
models.description: The polite pronoun and the request marker can make an exchange more considerate, but neither is universally formal or required in every relationship. Choose them according to the setting, social distance, and local expectations. A grammatically polite request can still sound abrupt if tone or context is unsuitable.

examples.translation: Please give me a little water.

models.label: invite-to-sit
models.title: Invite someone to sit
models.description: A short, context-sensitive invitation built with the polite request pattern.

models.label: choose-tea-politely
models.title: Ask, choose, and respond
models.description: A host asks about coffee, the guest chooses tea, and both close the offer politely.

utterance.translation: Do you want to drink coffee?

models.label: request-little-water
models.title: Make a polite water request
models.description: Combine the polite request frame with a small, nonspecific amount.
models.prompt: Politely ask someone to give you a little water.

answer.translation: Please give me a little water.

models.explanation: Put the polite request marker before the action. The small-amount expression comes directly before the drink.

models.label: number-sequence-listening
models.title: Hear number sequences as ordered chunks
models.description: First identify the number of items and their order, then compare individual syllables. Citation pinyin remains a dictionary guide; connected number sequences may have different rhythm or locally adjusted tone shapes. Preserve the sequence rather than judging a whole response from one unfamiliar sound.

models.label: two-cups-as-objects
models.title: Count two cups
models.description: Count cup objects with the general classifier and the pre-classifier form of *two*.

models.label: build-two-cup-count
models.title: Build a classifier phrase
models.description: Select the natural form of *two* before a classifier.
models.prompt: Say *two cups*, meaning two cup objects.
models.explanation: Use the pre-classifier form of *two*, followed by the general classifier and then the noun.

models.label: ask-cup-count
models.title: Ask how many cups
models.description: Ask for a small or expected count while keeping the classifier before the noun.

models.label: ask-for-cup-count
models.title: Ask for an unknown cup count
models.description: Replace the known number with the small-quantity question word.
models.prompt: Ask how many cup objects there are.
models.explanation: Keep the classifier between the quantity question word and the noun.

models.label: colloquial-currency-context
models.title: A practical spoken currency unit
models.description: In a mainland China price exchange, the colloquial unit in this example refers to one yuan of renminbi. The number before it gives the amount, so this example quotes three yuan. Establish the currency from the setting rather than assuming the same unit everywhere Chinese is spoken. These are sample prices, not current market prices or exchange rates.

models.label: two-cups-of-coffee
models.title: Specify two cups of coffee
models.description: Use the cupful classifier to count servings rather than empty cup objects.

models.label: buy-two-coffees
models.title: Order coffee and ask the price
models.description: A customer requests two servings, asks the price, and receives a concise price answer.

utterance.translation: Please give me two cups of coffee.

models.label: buy-two-cup-objects
models.title: Buy cups and ask the price
models.description: A customer states a desire to buy two cup objects and receives a price.

utterance.translation: I want to buy two cups.

models.label: answer-with-thirty-yuan
models.title: Give a sample price
models.description: Respond to a price question with a complete tens amount and the spoken currency unit.
models.prompt: Hear the price question, then reply with a sample price of thirty yuan.
models.explanation: Form the tens value with *three* before *ten*, then add the colloquial currency unit and the word for money.
